title: What If You Woke Up With a Foreign Accent? About 100 People Have

scenes.text: What if you woke up speaking in a foreign accent? You wouldn't have learned a thing.
Oslo, 1941. A woman is hit by shrapnel in an air raid. The left side of her brain is injured.

scenes.text: When she can speak again, her Norwegian sounds German. In occupied Norway, shopkeepers refuse to serve her.
It's called foreign accent syndrome. Doctors first described it in 1907, and only about a hundred cases are on record.
Nothing foreign is learned. Damage to the brain's speech centers shifts the vowels, the pitch and the rhythm.
Listeners' brains do the rest and hear an accent. For up to half of patients, the old voice returns on its own.

description:
What if you woke up speaking with a foreign accent? It has a name, foreign accent syndrome, first described in France in 1907; only about 100 cases have been reported in the scientific literature.
In the best-known case, a Norwegian woman hit by shrapnel in a 1941 air raid on Oslo began to sound German and was shunned in local shops. The person has not gained a language or a real accent: injury to the brain's speech centres, usually from a stroke or head injury, changes vowels, pitch and rhythm, and listeners hear that as foreign. Between 20 and 50 percent of patients recover their old accent naturally.
